location.title: Where Is Zinneke Pis?
location.answer: Zinneke Pis stands on the pavement outside number 35 on Rue des Chartreux in central Brussels, in the Chartreux (Kartuizers) district. It is a small bronze sculpture set against a lamppost, and it takes about 10 minutes to walk there from Grand Place.

intro.title: About Zinneke Pis
intro.breadcrumbs: Het Zinneke → Brussels → Brussels-Capital Region → Belgium
intro.firstParagraph: Het Zinneke, commonly known as Zinneke Pis, is the famous bronze peeing dog statue on Rue des Chartreux in central Brussels. It is small, sits almost at knee height beside a lamppost, and is easy to walk past if you do not know it is there.
intro.nearbyText: From the statue you can walk to Manneken Pis in about 8 minutes, to Grand Place in about 10 minutes and to Jeanneke Pis in about 12 minutes, so it fits naturally into a short loop around the centre.
intro.description:
Het Zinneke shows a scruffy street dog lifting its leg against a lamppost. It was created in 1999 by Brussels sculptor Tom Frantzen and completes the set of three 'Pis' figures in the city centre, next to Manneken Pis (1619) and Jeanneke Pis (1987).

The word 'Zinneke' comes from Brussels dialect and describes a mongrel born from a city dog and a village dog — a joke that Brussels people use about themselves. That is why the statue reads less as a monument and more as a wink at everyday city life.

Most visitors spend five to ten minutes here. There is nothing to buy and nothing is fenced off: the dog simply stands on a narrow street of cafés, food shops and cobblestones, a few steps away from the busy shopping streets but noticeably calmer.

knowledge.title: History and Meaning of Het Zinneke

sections.title: What Is the Peeing Dog Statue in Brussels?
sections.content:
The famous peeing dog statue in Brussels is Het Zinneke, better known as Zinneke Pis. It is a bronze sculpture of a mongrel dog urinating against a lamppost, installed in 1999 on Rue des Chartreux in the Chartreux district, roughly a 10-minute walk from Grand Place.

It is much smaller than most visitors expect — roughly the size of a real dog — so look down at the base of the lamppost rather than scanning the rooftops. Its official Google Maps listing name is 'Het Zinneke', which is why searches for the Dutch name return pictures of the same bronze dog.

sections.title: What Does "Zinneke" Mean?
sections.content:
In Brussels dialect the word 'Zinneke' described a mongrel: a dog born from a city dog and a village dog, a street animal of mixed origin. 'Zinne' itself echoes the Senne (Zenne), the river that runs through the city.

The word became a nickname for the mixed population of Brussels and for the Brusseleir identity — neither purely Dutch-speaking nor purely French-speaking. That double meaning is the whole joke of the statue: a small mixed-breed dog is a more honest emblem of Brussels than any official monument.

sections.title: History and Creation
sections.content:
Het Zinneke was created in 1999 by Tom Frantzen, a Brussels sculptor known for his humorous bronze animals. Visit Brussels lists the work as being part of the city's contemporary public art in the Chartreux district.

Frantzen gave the dog a deliberately casual pose, caught mid-movement, which is why it reads as a snapshot rather than a formal monument. The statue sits directly on the street instead of a plinth, so passers-by can walk right up to it.

sections.title: The Three Pis Statues of Brussels
sections.content:
Zinneke Pis is the third of Brussels' 'Pis' figures:

1. Manneken Pis (1619) — the little boy, the best known of the three
2. Jeanneke Pis (1987) — the little girl in the Impasse de la Fidélité
3. Het Zinneke / Zinneke Pis (1999) — the dog, the newest of the three

They are all within roughly a 15-minute walk of each other, which makes it possible to see all three in one loop starting and ending at Grand Place.

sections.title: About the Artist
sections.content:
Tom Frantzen (born 1954) is a Belgian sculptor whose public works include animals, figures and fountain groups in Brussels and other Belgian cities. His style is narrative and often comic, with movement exaggerated enough to read from a distance.

Het Zinneke is his best-known small work because it is installed at eye level on a street that thousands of people walk every day.

tickets.title: Tickets and Cost
tickets.guidedPrice: Five to ten minutes on site is enough; no guide or reservation is needed.
tickets.parkingPrice: Limited street parking. De Brouckère or the Grand Place car parks are a short walk away, and metro De Brouckère is about 8 minutes on foot.

transport.title: How to Get to Zinneke Pis
transport.fromCenterDesc: Leave Grand Place by Rue au Beurre, continue along Rue des Bouchers or Rue Grétry, then turn into Rue des Chartreux. The dog is on the pavement at number 35.
transport.fromStationDesc: From the station walk to Grand Place, then follow Rue au Beurre and Rue des Chartreux. The whole walk is about 15 minutes at normal pace.
transport.publicTransportDesc: Metro lines 1 and 5 stop at De Brouckère, about an 8-minute walk away. Bus routes to De Brouckère or Bourse stop just south of the statue.
transport.walkingDesc: Grand Place → Manneken Pis → Jeanneke Pis → Het Zinneke → Grand Place can be done in roughly 45–60 minutes without rushing.
transport.drivingDesc: The street is narrow and central Brussels has a low-emission zone. Parking under Grand Place or at De Brouckère and walking is simpler.
transport.fromAirportDesc: Train to Brussels-Central takes about 20 minutes, then walk 15 minutes, or take the metro one stop to De Brouckère and walk from there.

route.title: Recommended Walking Route Around Zinneke Pis
route.overview: Start at Grand Place, add the two other Pis statues, and finish back in the centre. With photo stops and a café break the loop takes about two hours.
steps: Start at Grand Place and admire the Town Hall and guild houses
Walk down Rue au Beurre to Manneken Pis (about 5 minutes)
Continue into Impasse de la Fidélité for Jeanneke Pis (about 3 minutes)
Walk north through the shopping streets to Rue des Chartreux
Find Het Zinneke at number 35 and take your photos (about 8 minutes from Manneken Pis)
Browse the Chartreux district — food shops, cafés and cobblestone lanes
Return to Grand Place via Rue des Bouchers (about 10 minutes)
End on a terrace at Grand Place with waffles or Belgian beer

faq.title: Frequently Asked Questions about Zinneke Pis

items.question: Where is Zinneke Pis located?
items.answer: Zinneke Pis stands outside number 35 on Rue des Chartreux, 1000 Brussels, in the Chartreux district. It is about a 10-minute walk from Grand Place. Plus Code: R8XW+G7 Brussels.

items.question: Is Zinneke Pis free to visit?
items.answer: Yes. Het Zinneke is an open-air street statue with no ticket, no fence and no opening hours, so you can see it at any time of day.

items.question: When was Zinneke Pis created?
items.answer: The bronze was created in 1999 by Brussels sculptor Tom Frantzen, according to Visit Brussels.

items.question: What is the peeing dog statue in Brussels called?
items.answer: It is called Het Zinneke and is also known as Zinneke Pis. Its Google Maps listing uses 'Het Zinneke', while 'Zinneke Pis' is the name most visitors search for.

items.question: What does “Zinneke” mean?
items.answer: In Brussels dialect, 'Zinneke' was a mongrel dog — the result of crossing a city dog with a village dog. The word became a nickname for the mixed population of Brussels and for local Brusseleir identity.

items.question: How do I get to Zinneke Pis from Grand Place?
items.answer: Leave Grand Place via Rue au Beurre, continue north and turn into Rue des Chartreux. The statue is on the pavement at number 35, roughly 10 minutes away. Metro De Brouckère is about 8 minutes' walk from it.

items.question: How long should I spend at Zinneke Pis?
items.answer: Most visitors spend five to ten minutes. There is no queue and no interior to visit, so it is best combined with Manneken Pis, Jeanneke Pis and Grand Place on one walk.

items.question: Are Manneken Pis and Jeanneke Pis nearby?
items.answer: Yes. Manneken Pis is about a 8-minute walk away, Jeanneke Pis about 12 minutes, and Grand Place about 10 minutes. All three can be seen on one loop.

items.question: Can I take photos at Zinneke Pis?
items.answer: Yes, photography is free and unrestricted. Morning is quietest, and because the statue sits on a working street you should stay on the pavement when composing a shot.

topicStatues.pageTitle: Brussels' 3 Famous Peeing Statues: Manneken, Jeanneke & Zinneke Pis
topicStatues.pageDescription: Compare the three Pis statues of Brussels: Manneken Pis (1619), Jeanneke Pis (1987) and Het Zinneke / Zinneke Pis (1999). Locations, walking distances and how to see all three in one loop.
topicStatues.title: Brussels' 3 Famous Peeing Statues
topicStatues.intro: Brussels has three statues famous for doing the same thing. Manneken Pis is the little boy everybody photographs, Jeanneke Pis is the little girl tucked into an alley, and Het Zinneke — better known as Zinneke Pis — is the dog. They sit within about fifteen minutes' walk of each other, so a single loop covers all three.
topicStatues.factsTitle: The three statues at a glance

facts.label: Manneken Pis
facts.value: 1619 · Rue de l'Étuve / Rue du Chêne, next to Grand Place. Bronze figure, roughly 61 cm tall, and the most photographed spot in the city.

facts.label: Jeanneke Pis
facts.value: 1987 · Impasse de la Fidélité, a short alley near Manneken Pis. Smaller and much quieter than the boy.

facts.label: Het Zinneke / Zinneke Pis
facts.value: 1999 · Rue des Chartreux 35, in the Chartreux district. A bronze mongrel lifting its leg against a lamppost, about a 10-minute walk from Grand Place.

facts.label: Total walking distance
facts.value: Roughly 2 km for a Grand Place loop taking in all three, comfortably done in 45–60 minutes at a normal pace.

steps: Start at Grand Place, the obvious orientation point in the centre
Walk to Manneken Pis along Rue de l'Étuve (2 minutes)
Cut into Impasse de la Fidélité for Jeanneke Pis (3 minutes)
Head north through the shopping streets towards the Chartreux district
Finish at Het Zinneke on Rue des Chartreux 35 (about 8 minutes from Manneken Pis)
Walk back to Grand Place in 10 minutes for the end of the loop

faq.question: What are the three peeing statues in Brussels called?
faq.answer: Manneken Pis (the boy, 1619), Jeanneke Pis (the girl, 1987) and Het Zinneke, also known as Zinneke Pis (the dog, 1999).

faq.question: How far apart are the three Pis statues?
faq.answer: Manneken Pis and Jeanneke Pis are a couple of minutes apart. Manneken Pis to Het Zinneke is about a 8-minute walk, and Grand Place is about 10 minutes from Het Zinneke.

faq.question: Are all three free to visit?
faq.answer: Yes. All three stand on public streets with no ticket, no fence and no opening hours.

faq.question: Which Pis statue is the oldest?
faq.answer: Manneken Pis, first installed in 1619. Jeanneke Pis dates from 1987 and Het Zinneke from 1999.

faq.question: Where is the least crowded of the three?
faq.answer: Het Zinneke on Rue des Chartreux is usually the quietest. Jeanneke Pis also sees far fewer people than Manneken Pis.

faq.question: How long does it take to see all three?
faq.answer: Around 45 to 60 minutes of walking if you do not linger, or up to two hours with photo stops and a café break.

topicRoute.pageTitle: Zinneke Pis to Manneken Pis: Distance, Walking Route & Map
topicRoute.pageDescription: How far Zinneke Pis is from Manneken Pis in Brussels: roughly 0.6 km and an 8-minute walk, with step-by-step streets, transport alternatives and how to add Jeanneke Pis and Grand Place.
topicRoute.title: Zinneke Pis to Manneken Pis
topicRoute.intro: Zinneke Pis (Het Zinneke) and Manneken Pis are close enough to combine into one short walk. The route runs from Rue des Chartreux in the Chartreux district down through the shopping streets to Rue de l'Étuve next to Grand Place, and it is almost entirely flat.

facts.label: Walking distance
facts.value: Roughly 0.6 km from Rue des Chartreux 35 to Rue de l'Étuve, depending on which pavement you follow.

facts.label: Walking time
facts.value: Around 8 minutes at a normal pace, or 10–15 minutes with photo stops and street crossings.

facts.label: Difficulty
facts.value: Flat, paved city streets. Suitable for wheelchairs and pushchairs, though the pavements are busy in the afternoon.

facts.label: Alternative
facts.value: There is no useful public transport hop between the two: the walk is shorter than waiting for a tram.

facts.label: Add Jeanneke Pis
facts.value: From Manneken Pis continue into Impasse de la Fidélité, about 2 minutes further.

facts.label: Checked
facts.value: Route steps and distance reviewed against map routing in October 2026.

steps: Leave Het Zinneke at Rue des Chartreux 35 facing north along the street
Continue towards Rue Neuve, the main shopping street of central Brussels
Follow Rue Neuve south past the retail blocks
Turn towards Place de la Monnaie and continue into Rue Neuve's southern end
Angle into Rue du Marché aux Herbes or Rue des Fripiers towards the old centre
Turn towards Rue de l'Étuve — Manneken Pis is on the corner
Optional: continue into Impasse de la Fidélité for Jeanneke Pis

faq.question: How far is Zinneke Pis from Manneken Pis?
faq.answer: Roughly 0.6 km, or about an 8-minute walk along flat city streets.

faq.question: Can I walk from Zinneke Pis to Manneke Pis?
faq.answer: Yes. The whole route is on public pavements and takes under ten minutes. It is the simplest way to link the two statues.

faq.question: Is there a metro or tram between them?
faq.answer: Taking public transport is not worth it for such a short distance, but metro De Brouckère is the nearest station to both, sitting between the two statues.

faq.question: How do I get from Zinneke Pis to Jeanneke Pis?
faq.answer: Walk first to Manneken Pis (about 8 minutes), then continue into Impasse de la Fidélité, roughly 2 more minutes.

faq.question: Is the route wheelchair accessible?
faq.answer: The streets are paved and level, but central pavements can be crowded and narrow in places. Allow extra time in the afternoon.

faq.question: What else is on the way?
faq.answer: Rue Neuve shopping street, Place de la Monnaie and eventually Grand Place, which is about 10 minutes from Het Zinneke.

locationAndMap.title: Zinneke Pis: Location and Map
locationAndMap.intro: Het Zinneke is easy to walk past because it is small and sits at street level. This page gives the exact address, the coordinates and Plus Code used by the map links, what to look for on the street, and the closest metro stops — so you can reach it without circling the block.

sections.title: The exact spot
sections.body:
Zinneke Pis stands on the pavement outside number 35 on Rue des Chartreux, in the Chartreux district (Kartuizerswijk) of central Brussels, postal code 1000. The bronze dog leans against a lamppost at roughly knee height, so you will miss it if you scan the houses at eye level.

The street itself is narrow, cobbled in places and used by residents and delivery traffic. It is a working street rather than a pedestrian square, which is part of the statue's charm — and the reason you should stay on the pavement when you step back for photos.

sections.title: Coordinates and Plus Code
sections.body:
The map links on this site use latitude 50.84879 and longitude 4.32664, with Plus Code R8XW+G7. These match the public Google Maps listing, which is filed under the name 'Het Zinneke'.

If your map app drops you at the wrong end of the street, walk towards number 35: the statue is on the pavement beside the lamppost, not on a corner or in a square.

sections.title: How to recognise the right street
sections.body:
Rue des Chartreux — Kartuizersstraat in Dutch — runs through a quiet district of small food shops, cafés and housing between the busy Rue Neuve shopping street and the Antoine Dansaert quarter.

The statue sits on the more central end of the street. If you reach the quieter residential lanes further north or a canal-side street, you have gone too far.

sections.title: Nearest metro stops and stations
sections.body:
The closest metro station is De Brouckère (lines 1 and 5), about an 8-minute walk from the statue. Brussels-Central railway station is slightly further, at 10–12 minutes on foot.

Several bus lines cross the boulevards just south of the street, but no tram stops beside the statue. Check the current STIB/MIVB network before travelling.

faq.question: Where exactly is Zinneke Pis?
faq.answer: On the pavement outside number 35 on Rue des Chartreux, 1000 Brussels, beside a lamppost. It is about a 10-minute walk from Grand Place.

faq.question: What is the Plus Code for Zinneke Pis?
faq.answer: R8XW+G7 Brussels, Belgium. Typing it into Google Maps places the pin at the statue.

faq.question: Why can't I find it on Google Maps?
faq.answer: Search for 'Het Zinneke' rather than 'Zinneke Pis': that is the name the public listing uses, and the pin drops you on Rue des Chartreux at number 35.

faq.question: How do I know I am on the right street?
faq.answer: Rue des Chartreux is a narrow, partly cobbled street of small shops and cafés in the Chartreux district, just north of the Rue Neuve shopping street.

faq.question: What is the nearest metro station?
faq.answer: De Brouckère on lines 1 and 5, about 8 minutes away. Brussels-Central station is about 10–12 minutes on foot.

faq.question: Is there parking at the statue?
faq.answer: No. The street has no visitor parking. The nearest public car parks are under Grand Place and at De Brouckère.

publicTransport.pageTitle: How to Get to Zinneke Pis by Metro, Bus and Train
publicTransport.pageDescription: Public transport to Zinneke Pis in Brussels: the nearest metro stop De Brouckère, train connections from Central and Midi stations, bus and night services, and how tickets work.
publicTransport.title: Getting to Zinneke Pis by Public Transport
publicTransport.intro: Zinneke Pis sits in the middle of central Brussels, so most visitors arrive on foot from Grand Place or from a nearby station. This page compares the realistic options: metro, train, bus, night services and tickets.

sections.title: Metro: De Brouckère is the best stop
sections.body:
De Brouckère station (lines 1 and 5) is the closest metro stop to the statue, about an 8-minute walk away. From there, follow Rue Neuve north and turn into Rue des Chartreux.

Brussels-Central station is served by the same lines 1 and 5 and is a slightly longer walk of 10–12 minutes, but it is useful if you arrive by train.

sections.title: By train: Central and Midi stations
sections.body:
From Brussels-Central, either walk (about 15 minutes) or take line 1 or 5 one stop to De Brouckère and walk from there.

From Brussels-Midi — the Eurostar and Thalys terminal — take metro line 2 or 6 to Arts-Loi, change to line 1 or 5 towards De Brouckère, then walk about 8 minutes. Allow roughly 25 minutes for the whole trip. Check STIB/MIVB for engineering works before you travel.

sections.title: Bus and tram
sections.body:
No tram stops directly beside the statue. Several bus lines run along the boulevards and the Rue Neuve area a few minutes south of the street, including stops near De Brouckère and Bourse.

For current routes and times, use the official operator's journey planner rather than a third-party app.

sections.title: Tickets and fares
sections.body:
A single STIB/MIVB ticket covers metro, tram and bus for one hour with transfers, and contactless bank cards are accepted at metro gates. If you plan to visit several sights, a day pass is usually cheaper than return singles.

Walking is genuinely competitive here: the statue is only about 10 minutes from Grand Place, so most visitors do not need public transport at all once they are in the centre.

sections.title: Late at night
sections.body: Metro services stop around midnight, with the Noctis night network running on weekend nights. At other times a taxi or rideshare from the centre is the practical option, and the walk from Grand Place is short and well lit.

faq.answer: Take metro line 2 or 6 to Arts-Loi, change to line 1 or 5 to De Brouckère, then walk about 8 minutes — roughly 25 minutes in total.

faq.question: How do I get from Central Station?

faq.question: Do I need a paper ticket?
faq.answer: No. Contactless bank cards work at metro gates, and single tickets cover metro, tram and bus for one hour with transfers.

faq.question: Is public transport running late at night?
faq.answer: Metro stops around midnight; the Noctis night network runs on weekend nights. Otherwise taxis or rideshares from the centre are the practical option.

grandPlaceRoute.pageTitle: Grand Place to Zinneke Pis: Walking Route, Distance and Time
grandPlaceRoute.pageDescription: Walk from Brussels' Grand Place to Zinneke Pis in about 10 minutes: the route, the roughly 0.8 km distance, the streets to follow and what you pass on the way.
grandPlaceRoute.title: Grand Place to Zinneke Pis on Foot
grandPlaceRoute.intro: Grand Place is the natural starting point for a visit to Zinneke Pis. The walk is short, flat and almost entirely through the old centre — about 0.8 km and 10 minutes at a normal pace.

sections.title: The route in short
sections.body:
Leave Grand Place by Rue au Beurre on its northern side, keep going north and continue into Rue des Chartreux. The statue is on the pavement at number 35, against the lamppost.

There is no steep grade and no complicated junction: if you keep the general direction north and watch for the street name, you will arrive without a map.

sections.title: What you will pass
sections.body: You start between the guild houses of Grand Place, pass through streets of small shops and restaurants, and finish on a quieter cobbled street of food shops and cafés. The change in atmosphere is part of the point: the busy tourist centre gives way to a working neighbourhood within a few hundred metres.

sections.title: Surfaces and step-free access
sections.body: The route is on paved and partly cobbled city streets and is essentially flat. Most of it is step-free, but old Brussels pavements can have raised kerbs and narrow sections — wheelchair users and people with pushchairs should allow a little extra time, especially on Rue des Chartreux itself.

sections.title: A slightly longer alternative
sections.body: If you prefer shopping streets, go via Rue Neuve instead: it adds a few minutes and a lot of shops, and joins Rue des Chartreux at its southern end. The quieter Rue au Beurre route is the one most guides use.

steps: Stand with your back to Grand Place's Town Hall and find Rue au Beurre on the northern side of the square
Follow Rue au Beurre north out of the square
Continue straight into Rue des Chartreux, keeping north
Walk along the cobbled street past the small shops and cafés
The statue is on the pavement at number 35, beside the lamppost

faq.question: How far is Grand Place from Zinneke Pis?
faq.answer: Roughly 0.8 km, or about a 10-minute walk through the old centre.

faq.question: Which street do I take from Grand Place?
faq.answer: Rue au Beurre on the northern side of the square, then continue north into Rue des Chartreux to number 35.

faq.question: Is the walk suitable for wheelchairs?
faq.answer: It is flat and paved, though partly cobbled with some raised kerbs. Allow extra time on the narrower sections of Rue des Chartreux.

faq.question: Can I combine it with Manneken Pis?
faq.answer: Yes. Manneken Pis is on the way between Grand Place and the Chartreux district if you take the Rue Neuve route, and is about 8 minutes from Het Zinneke in the other direction.

faq.question: Is there a shorter way?
faq.answer: The streets form a grid, so small variations exist, but nothing meaningfully shortens the walk. About 0.8 km is the realistic minimum.

centralStationRoute.pageTitle: Brussels Central Station to Zinneke Pis: Walking Directions
centralStationRoute.pageDescription: How to walk from Brussels-Central railway station to Zinneke Pis in about 15 minutes: the route via Mont des Arts and Grand Place, distance, step-free notes and the metro alternative.
centralStationRoute.title: Brussels Central Station to Zinneke Pis on Foot
centralStationRoute.intro: If you arrive at Brussels-Central by train, the statue is an easy walk away. This page gives a route that works, the distance and time, and a one-stop metro alternative for anyone with luggage.

sections.title: The route on foot
sections.body:
Leave the station by the main exit onto Boulevard de l'Impératrice, walk up towards Mont des Arts and take the slope or steps down via Rue Montagne de la Cour to the edge of Grand Place. From there, follow Rue au Beurre north into Rue des Chartreux to number 35.

The whole walk is about 15 minutes and 1.2 km. It is one of several possible routes through the centre, but it uses recognisable landmarks at every stage.

sections.title: Distance and time
sections.body: Roughly 1.2 km, or about 15 minutes at a normal pace with traffic lights. The route is flat apart from the short descent from Mont des Arts to Grand Place, where lifts and ramps are available as an alternative to the steps.

sections.title: With luggage
sections.body: Cobbles and crowded pavements make the full walk uncomfortable with suitcases. In that case take metro line 1 or 5 one stop from Gare Centrale to De Brouckère, then walk about 8 minutes — around 20 minutes door to door.

sections.title: By metro instead
sections.body: Gare Centrale is on lines 1 and 5, the same lines that serve De Brouckère. One stop separates them, and the walk from De Brouckère to the statue is about 8 minutes along Rue Neuve and Rue des Chartreux.

steps: Leave Brussels-Central station by the main exit onto Boulevard de l'Impératrice
Walk up towards Mont des Arts, then down via Rue Montagne de la Cour towards Grand Place
Cross the edge of Grand Place and find Rue au Beurre on its northern side
Follow Rue au Beurre north and continue into Rue des Chartreux
The statue is on the pavement at number 35, beside the lamppost

faq.question: How far is Brussels-Central station from Zinneke Pis?
faq.answer: About 1.2 km, or a 15-minute walk through Mont des Arts and Grand Place.

faq.question: Can I take the metro from Central Station?
faq.answer: Yes. Lines 1 and 5 run from Gare Centrale to De Brouckère in one stop; the statue is about 8 minutes' walk from De Brouckère.

faq.question: Is the walk step-free?
faq.answer: Almost. The descent from Mont des Arts to Grand Place has steps, but lifts and ramps provide an alternative.

faq.question: What is the easiest landmark to navigate by?
faq.answer: Aim for Mont des Arts first, then Grand Place, then Rue au Beurre — each is well signposted for pedestrians.

faq.question: Should I walk if I have a suitcase?
faq.answer: No. Take the metro to De Brouckère instead; cobbles and crowded pavements make walking with luggage unpleasant.

midiStationRoute.pageTitle: Brussels Midi Station to Zinneke Pis: Metro, Walk or Taxi
midiStationRoute.pageDescription: How to get from Brussels-Midi (Gare du Midi / Zuidstation) to Zinneke Pis: metro with one change at Arts-Loi, the walking route and distance, and notes for Eurostar arrivals.
midiStationRoute.title: Brussels Midi Station to Zinneke Pis
midiStationRoute.intro: Brussels-Midi is where Eurostar and Thalys trains arrive, and it is the busiest station in the country — but it is south of the centre, so reaching Zinneke Pis takes planning. Here are the realistic options.

sections.title: By metro: about 25 minutes
sections.body:
Take metro line 2 or 6 from Gare du Midi to Arts-Loi, change to line 1 or 5 towards De Brouckère, then walk about 8 minutes to the statue. The whole trip takes roughly 25 minutes including the change.

This is the option most visitors use. Check the STIB/MIVB journey planner on the day, because weekend engineering works can change the pattern.

sections.title: On foot: about 30 minutes
sections.body:
The walk from Gare du Midi to Rue des Chartreux is about 2.2 km and takes roughly 30 minutes. It runs mostly straight north through the city centre — possible in good weather, but not the most interesting stretch of Brussels for a first walk.

If you do walk, follow the boulevards north and turn towards Rue Neuve when you reach the centre, or use the Google Maps walking directions linked below.

sections.title: By taxi or rideshare
sections.body:
A taxi from the station ranks takes about 10 minutes in normal traffic, longer at rush hour. Rideshare pick-up points are signposted at the station.

Central Brussels has a low-emission zone, but this does not affect short passenger trips — it matters only if you drive yourself.

sections.title: Arriving by Eurostar or Thalys
sections.body: Leave the secure area, follow the metro signs for lines 2 and 6, and follow the route above. Ticket gates accept contactless cards, so you do not need to queue for a paper ticket.

faq.answer: Take metro line 2 or 6 to Arts-Loi, change to line 1 or 5 to De Brouckère, then walk about 8 minutes — roughly 25 minutes in total.

faq.question: How long is the walk from Midi station?
faq.answer: About 2.2 km and 30 minutes, mostly straight north through the centre.

faq.question: Is a taxi expensive?
faq.answer: It is a short city trip of about 10 minutes, so it is a reasonable option with luggage or at night, but the metro is cheaper and usually faster at rush hour.

faq.question: I arrive by Eurostar — what is the simplest plan?
faq.answer: Follow the metro signs for lines 2 and 6, ride to Arts-Loi, change to line 1 or 5 to De Brouckère, and walk 8 minutes.

jeannekeRoute.pageTitle: Zinneke Pis to Jeanneke Pis: Walking Route, Distance and Time
jeannekeRoute.pageDescription: How far Zinneke Pis is from Jeanneke Pis in Brussels and how to walk it: the route via Manneken Pis, about 0.8 km and 10–12 minutes, with step-by-step directions.
jeannekeRoute.title: Zinneke Pis to Jeanneke Pis on Foot
jeannekeRoute.intro: Zinneke Pis and Jeanneke Pis are the two quietest of Brussels' three Pis statues, and they are close enough to link in one short walk. The natural route passes Manneken Pis on the way.

sections.title: The route
sections.body:
From Rue des Chartreux 35, walk south towards Rue Neuve, follow it towards Place de la Monnaie, then cut into the old centre via Rue du Marché aux Herbes or Rue des Fripiers. Turn towards Rue de l'Étuve to reach Manneken Pis on its corner, then continue a few steps into Impasse de la Fidélité for Jeanneke Pis.

The whole walk is about 0.8 km and 10–12 minutes, almost entirely flat.

sections.title: What to expect at Jeanneke Pis
sections.body:
Jeanneke Pis is smaller and far less visited than Manneken Pis. She sits in a narrow alley on a low base, so she is easy to miss even when you are in the right street. Look for the alley entrance rather than scanning for a crowd.

The alley is a public passage, open at all hours and free to visit.

sections.title: Combining all three Pis statues
sections.body:
A loop that starts at Grand Place, takes in Manneken Pis, Jeanneke Pis and Het Zinneke, and returns to Grand Place covers roughly 2 km in 45–60 minutes without rushing.

Doing it in the order Grand Place → Manneken Pis → Jeanneke Pis → Het Zinneke keeps the two quiet statues before the busiest streets.

steps: Leave Het Zinneke at Rue des Chartreux 35 and head south towards Rue Neuve
Follow Rue Neuve south past the shopping blocks towards Place de la Monnaie
Turn into Rue du Marché aux Herbes or Rue des Fripiers towards the old centre
Reach Rue de l'Étuve — Manneken Pis stands on the corner
Continue a few steps into Impasse de la Fidélité — Jeanneke Pis is in the alley

faq.question: How far is Zinneke Pis from Jeanneke Pis?
faq.answer: About 0.8 km, or 10–12 minutes on foot via Manneken Pis.

faq.question: Do I have to pass Manneken Pis?
faq.answer: You do not have to stop, but the natural route passes its corner — the two statues are only 2–3 minutes apart.

faq.question: Where exactly is Jeanneke Pis?
faq.answer: In the Impasse de la Fidélité, a narrow alley a short walk from Manneken Pis and Grand Place.

faq.question: Is the route wheelchair accessible?
faq.answer: The streets are flat and paved, though busy and narrow in places. The alley itself is a public passage.

faq.question: Can I see all three Pis statues in one walk?
faq.answer: Yes. Grand Place → Manneken Pis → Jeanneke Pis → Het Zinneke → Grand Place is roughly 2 km and takes 45–60 minutes.

history.pageTitle: Zinneke Pis History: The 1998/1999 Question and Tom Frantzen
history.pageDescription: The history of Zinneke Pis (Het Zinneke) in Brussels: what is documented, why some sources list 1998 and others 1999, and the story behind the bronze dog on Rue des Chartreux.
history.title: The History of Zinneke Pis
history.intro: Zinneke Pis is a recent work compared with Manneken Pis, but it already carries its own small legend. This page separates what is documented from what is folklore — including the 1998 versus 1999 question that even official sources do not agree on.

sections.title: What is documented
sections.body:
Visit Brussels, the official tourism body for the Brussels-Capital Region, lists Het Zinneke (Zinneke-Pis) as a work by the Brussels sculptor Tom Frantzen dated 1999, installed at Rue des Chartreux 35. The public Google Maps listing for the statue uses the name 'Het Zinneke' and the same address.

The sculpture itself is a small bronze figure of a mongrel dog lifting its leg against a lamppost, set directly on the street without a plinth.

sections.title: Why some sources say 1998
sections.body:
Tom Frantzen's own website lists the work with the year 1998, while Visit Brussels gives 1999. Both dates circulate online, and this guide shows 1999 because it follows the official tourism listing for the address.

We deliberately do not turn the difference into a story such as 'created in 1998, installed in 1999' — there is no reliable evidence for that sequence. Where older pages mention 1998, current official information points to 1999, and the artist's own dating is the other live source. Until the two are reconciled by a primary document, showing the discrepancy is the honest option.

sections.title: The third Pis
sections.body:
Brussels already had a peeing boy and a peeing girl when Frantzen added a dog. Manneken Pis dates from 1619 and is the city's best-known statue; Jeanneke Pis followed in 1987 as a deliberate counterpoint.

Het Zinneke completed the set in the late 1990s, and its joke is different: where the boy is a landmark and the girl a statement, the dog is a self-portrait of the city as a mixed-breed mongrel.

sections.title: The street and its name
sections.body:
Rue des Chartreux takes its name from the Carthusian monks — the Chartreux — whose order was present in this part of Brussels. The district, the Kartuizerswijk, kept the name long after the religious houses disappeared.

The street Frantzen chose for the statue is a working one: small food shops, cafés and housing rather than a tourist square. That choice is consistent with the humour of the work.

faq.question: When was Zinneke Pis made?
faq.answer: Visit Brussels dates it to 1999; Tom Frantzen's own website lists 1998. This guide shows 1999 and notes the discrepancy rather than inventing an explanation.

faq.question: Who created Zinneke Pis?
faq.answer: Tom Frantzen, a Brussels sculptor known for humorous bronze figures and animals in public spaces.

faq.question: Why do some websites say 1998?
faq.answer: Because the artist's own site uses that year, and many pages copied it. Official tourism information currently points to 1999.

faq.question: Was Zinneke Pis inspired by Manneken Pis?
faq.answer: It is a response to the tradition rather than a copy: same city, same joke, different animal. Manneken Pis dates from 1619, Het Zinneke from around 1999.

faq.question: Has the statue been moved or replaced?
faq.answer: It still stands at its original address on Rue des Chartreux. Street statues in Brussels are occasionally restored or cleaned, but there is no documented replacement of this work.

faq.question: Why is it called Zinneke?
faq.answer: 'Zinneke' is a Brussels dialect word for a mongrel dog, which became a nickname for the city's mixed population — the joke the statue makes about itself.

zinnekeMeaning.pageTitle: What Does 'Zinneke' Mean? The Brussels Dialect Word Explained
zinnekeMeaning.pageDescription: The meaning of 'Zinneke' in Brussels dialect: mongrel dog, the Senne river and Brusseleir identity — and why the bronze dog on Rue des Chartreux carries the name.
zinnekeMeaning.title: What Does 'Zinneke' Mean?
zinnekeMeaning.intro: The name is the whole point of the statue. 'Zinneke' is a Brussels dialect word, and understanding it explains why a small peeing dog became an emblem of the city.

sections.title: The word itself
sections.body:
In Brussels dialect, a 'zinneke' was a mongrel: a dog born from a city dog and a village dog, an animal of mixed origin with no pedigree. The word is linked to the Senne — the Zenne — the river that runs through Brussels, and to the street life that grew around it.

Calling someone a zinneke was never purely an insult. It described a mixed background, and Brusselers applied it to themselves with some pride.

sections.title: From mongrel to city identity
sections.body:
Over time 'zinneke' became a nickname for the mixed population of Brussels itself — a city that is neither purely Dutch-speaking nor purely French-speaking, but a blend of both plus everything that arrived through its port and its industries.

That is why the word sticks to the statue: a scruffy street dog of no particular breed is a more honest emblem of Brussels than any grand monument.

sections.title: How the statue uses the joke
sections.body:
Frantzen's dog is deliberately unheroic. It is small, caught mid-movement, and set against a lamppost on an ordinary street rather than raised on a plinth in a square. Visitors who expect a monument are surprised by a mutt.

The humour is typical of Brussels' 'zwanze': the local habit of mocking yourself before anyone else can.

sections.title: Related names and spellings
sections.body:
The statue is known as Het Zinneke ('the mutt'), Zinneke Pis ('the mutt that pees') and Zinneke-Pis. Its Google Maps listing uses 'Het Zinneke', while most visitors search for 'Zinneke Pis'.

In Dutch it is sometimes written Zinneke Pis Brussel or simply het zinnepisbeeld; in French, Zinneke Pis Bruxelles or le chien qui fait pipi. All of these refer to the same bronze dog.

facts.label: Literal meaning
facts.value: Mongrel — a dog of mixed city and village origin

facts.label: Language
facts.value: Brussels dialect (Brusseleir), with links to the Senne/Zenne river

facts.label: Figurative meaning
facts.value: A nickname for Brussels' mixed population and identity

facts.label: Statue names
facts.value: Het Zinneke, Zinneke Pis, Zinneke-Pis — all the same bronze dog

faq.question: What does 'zinneke' mean in Dutch?
faq.answer: A mongrel dog — specifically one born from a city dog and a village dog. In Brussels dialect it also came to describe the city's mixed population.

faq.question: Is 'zinneke' an insult?
faq.answer: It can be used sharply, but Brusselers use it about themselves with pride. Applied to the statue it is affectionate.

faq.question: What does Zinneke Pis literally mean?
faq.answer: Roughly 'the mongrel that pees' — the same naming pattern as Manneken Pis ('the little man who pees') and Jeanneke Pis.

faq.question: Why is a mongrel a symbol of Brussels?
faq.answer: Because the city sees itself as a mix: of languages, of neighbourhoods, of arrivals. The dog is a self-mocking emblem of that mixture.

faq.question: What language is Brusseleir?
faq.answer: A local dialect of Dutch spoken in Brussels, with French influences and its own vocabulary — the source of words like 'zinneke'.

photos.pageTitle: Zinneke Pis Photos: Best Angles, Times and What You Will See
photos.pageDescription: How to photograph Zinneke Pis (Het Zinneke) in Brussels: the angles that work, the quietest times of day, what the small bronze dog really looks like, and our own photo gallery.
photos.title: Photographing Zinneke Pis
photos.intro: Zinneke Pis is a difficult subject done right: it is small, it sits on a working street, and the light changes quickly between tall houses. This page covers what the statue really looks like, the angles that work, and when to shoot.

sections.title: What the statue really looks like
sections.body:
Het Zinneke is roughly the size of a real dog — much smaller than most visitors expect. It is a bronze mongrel with a curled tail, caught lifting its leg against a lamppost, with a slightly scruffy, humorous modelling that reads better up close than in wide shots.

Because it stands at knee height on the pavement, most photographs fail by being taken from too far away.

sections.title: Six angles that work
sections.body:
The front view shows the whole silhouette against the lamppost. A side angle captures the raised leg. A close-up on the head and tail shows the patina and modelling. Including the full lamppost shows the composition the sculptor intended.

Crossing the street and shooting wider places the dog in its cobbled setting, and after dark the street lighting picks out the bronze — though low light needs a higher ISO or a steady hand.

sections.title: When to shoot
sections.body:
Morning between 8 and 10 is the quietest time, with clean light on the bronze and few people in frame. Evenings from 18 to 20 give warmer light and open café terraces nearby. Winter middays offer the best natural light in the darker months.

The street has traffic, so stay on the pavement when you step back for a shot.

sections.title: Our gallery
sections.body:
This site publishes its own photographs of the statue and its street — front, side and detail views, plus the surrounding district in different seasons and at night. They are illustrative images taken on Rue des Chartreux.

This is an independent, non-commercial visitor guide. If you believe any image is mislabelled or should be credited or removed, please get in touch and we will correct it.

facts.value: Morning 8–10 for empty frames; evening 18–20 for warm light

facts.value: Free and unrestricted — it is a public street

facts.value: It is a live street: stay on the pavement, watch for traffic

faq.question: Can I take photos of Zinneke Pis?
faq.answer: Yes. Photography is free and unrestricted — the statue stands on a public street.

faq.question: What does Zinneke Pis actually look like?
faq.answer: A small bronze mongrel dog, roughly the size of a real dog, lifting its leg against a lamppost at knee height.

faq.question: When is the best time to photograph it?
faq.answer: Morning between 8 and 10, when the street is quiet and the light on the bronze is clean.

faq.question: Is it crowded?
faq.answer: Rarely busy compared with Manneken Pis. Afternoons bring more shoppers to the street, but you can almost always get a clear shot.

faq.question: Can I take photos at night?
faq.answer: Yes. Street lighting picks out the bronze, but low light needs a higher ISO, a tripod or a steady surface.

faq.question: Where do the photos on this site come from?
faq.answer: They are our own photographs taken on Rue des Chartreux. Corrections or credit requests are welcome — see the footer for contact details.

mannekenPis.pageTitle: Manneken Pis Guide: Location, Costumes and Visiting Tips
mannekenPis.pageDescription: Visiting Manneken Pis near Zinneke Pis: exact location, how far it is, the costume tradition and garderobe, where the original statue is kept, and practical tips.
mannekenPis.title: Manneken Pis: Visitor Guide
mannekenPis.intro: Manneken Pis is the statue everyone means when they talk about Brussels. It is also the closest major landmark to Zinneke Pis, about 8 minutes away — so most visitors see both. This guide covers what to expect and how to combine them.

sections.title: What it is and where
sections.body:
Manneken Pis is a small bronze figure of a boy, roughly 61 cm tall, standing on a fountain base at the corner of Rue de l'Étuve and Rue du Chêne, a few minutes' walk from Grand Place. The current version dates from a recasting in the 20th century: earlier statues were stolen or damaged, and the original medieval figure no longer stands in the street.

It is free, outdoors and accessible at any hour, though the surrounding streets are busiest in the afternoon.

sections.title: The costume tradition
sections.body:
Manneken Pis is dressed in costumes that change through the year — several hundred outfits have been given by cities, guilds and foreign states. The costume collection is kept and displayed at the Garderobe, the statue's wardrobe museum, a short walk away.

Whether the boy is dressed on the day of your visit depends on the schedule, so treat any costume as a bonus rather than the point of the visit.

sections.title: Where the original statue is
sections.body:
The original Manneken Pis is kept by the Brussels City Museum in the Maison du Roi on Grand Place, where it is displayed in a glass case. Visiting the street statue and the museum original on the same walk is the classic way to see both.

Check the museum's own site for opening times and admission before you go.

sections.title: Getting there from Zinneke Pis
sections.body:
The walk from Rue des Chartreux 35 to Manneken Pis is about 0.6 km and 8 minutes, via Rue Neuve and Place de la Monnaie. Doing Zinneke Pis → Manneken Pis → Grand Place in that order keeps the quiet statue first and the crowds last.

Our step-by-step route page covers the streets in detail.

faq.answer: About 0.6 km, or an 8-minute walk via Rue Neuve and Place de la Monnaie.

faq.question: Is Manneken Pis free to visit?
faq.answer: Yes. It stands on a public street with no ticket, no fence and no opening hours.

faq.question: Where is the original Manneken Pis?
faq.answer: In the Brussels City Museum in the Maison du Roi on Grand Place. The street statue is a later bronze.

faq.question: Will the statue be wearing a costume?
faq.answer: Maybe. Costumes change on a schedule kept by the city and the Garderobe museum; there is no guarantee on any given day.

faq.question: Why is Manneken Pis so famous?
faq.answer: It is old, tiny, irreverent and has been stolen, copied and dressed up for centuries — Brussels adopted it as its unofficial emblem.

faq.question: Is Manneken Pis bigger than Zinneke Pis?
faq.answer: They are similar in scale. Manneken Pis is roughly 61 cm on its base; Het Zinneke is closer to the size of a real dog at knee height.

jeannekePis.pageTitle: Jeanneke Pis: Location, How to Find It and Why It Was Made
jeannekePis.pageDescription: How to find Jeanneke Pis in Brussels: the alley location, how far it is from Zinneke Pis and Manneken Pis, what the small statue looks like and why it exists.
jeannekePis.title: Jeanneke Pis: Visitor Guide
jeannekePis.intro: Jeanneke Pis is the quietest of Brussels' three Pis statues — small, tucked into an alley, and easy to miss even when you know where you are going. This guide covers how to find her and why she was made.

sections.title: Where she is
sections.body:
Jeanneke Pis stands in the Impasse de la Fidélité, a narrow public alley a short walk from Manneken Pis. The alley entrance is easy to walk past: look for the gap between the buildings rather than for a crowd or a sign.

She is about 0.8 km and 10–12 minutes from Zinneke Pis on foot, and only 2–3 minutes from Manneken Pis.

sections.title: What she looks like
sections.body:
The statue is a small bronze figure of a girl, crouching slightly, set on a low base against the wall of the alley. It was installed in 1987 as a deliberate counterpoint to the centuries-old fame of Manneken Pis.

Because the alley is narrow, the best photographs are taken from directly in front, close up.

sections.title: Why she exists
sections.body:
By the 1980s Brussels' most famous statue was a boy, and the city's public art had little room for any other answer. Jeanneke Pis was commissioned to complete the joke — and, in the spirit of the zwanze, to laugh at the fame of the original at the same time.

She is often read as a small feminist statue, and she is certainly the least crowded of the three.

sections.title: Combining her with the other Pis statues
sections.body:
The classic loop is Grand Place → Manneken Pis → Jeanneke Pis → Het Zinneke → Grand Place, roughly 2 km in 45–60 minutes. Visiting Jeanneke Pis immediately after Manneken Pis adds only a few minutes.

Our walking route pages give the street-by-street directions for each leg.

faq.question: Why is Jeanneke Pis hard to find?
faq.answer: It is small, it sits in a narrow alley, and there is no crowd around it. Look for the alley entrance near Manneken Pis.

faq.question: When was Jeanneke Pis made?
faq.answer: In 1987, as a deliberate counterpoint to Manneken Pis.

faq.question: Is Jeanneke Pis free to visit?
faq.answer: Yes. She stands in a public alley with no ticket and no opening hours.

faq.question: Which of the three Pis statues is quietest?
faq.answer: Jeanneke Pis and Het Zinneke are both quiet compared with Manneken Pis; Jeanneke Pis sees the fewest visitors.

rueDesChartreux.pageTitle: Rue des Chartreux & the Chartreux District: Brussels Guide
rueDesChartreux.pageDescription: A guide to Rue des Chartreux (Kartuizersstraat) in Brussels: the street where Zinneke Pis stands, the Chartreux district, what to see, shops and cafés, and walking tips.
rueDesChartreux.title: Rue des Chartreux and the Chartreux District
rueDesChartreux.intro: The street is half the reason to visit Zinneke Pis. Rue des Chartreux — Kartuizersstraat in Dutch — is one of those central Brussels streets where the city feels local rather than touristic, and the statue is simply part of the furniture.

sections.title: The street
sections.body:
Rue des Chartreux runs through the Chartreux district (Kartuizerswijk), just north of the Rue Neuve shopping street and a few minutes east of the Antoine Dansaert quarter. It is narrow, partly cobbled, and lined with small food shops, cafés and housing.

The bronze dog stands on the pavement at number 35, against a lamppost — unmarked, unfenced and easy to miss.

sections.title: The district and its name
sections.body:
The street and district take their names from the Carthusian monks — the Chartreux — whose order was present in this part of Brussels for centuries. The Dutch name of the street, Kartuizersstraat, comes from the same root.

What remains today is a working neighbourhood: bakers, grocers, cafés and apartments, with the busier shopping streets a block away.

sections.title: What to see and do
sections.body:
Walk the length of the street rather than heading straight to the statue. Look at the shopfronts and the façades, then double back to the lamppost. The district rewards a slow ten minutes more than a fast photo stop.

From here you can continue to the Antoine Dansaert quarter for more shops and cafés, or cut back to Rue Neuve for the shopping streets.

sections.title: Practical tips
sections.body:
Morning is the quietest time on the street; afternoons bring shoppers from Rue Neuve. It is a live street with traffic and deliveries, so stay on the pavement when photographing the statue.

The nearest metro is De Brouckère, about 8 minutes away, and Grand Place is about 10 minutes on foot.

faq.question: What is the Dutch name of Rue des Chartreux?
faq.answer: Kartuizersstraat. Brussels street signs are bilingual, so you will see both names.

faq.question: Where is the Chartreux district?
faq.answer: In central Brussels, between the Rue Neuve shopping street and the Antoine Dansaert quarter, a few minutes north of Grand Place.

faq.question: Why is it called Chartreux?
faq.answer: The name comes from the Carthusian monks (Chartreux / Kartuizers) whose order was once present in this part of the city.

faq.question: What kind of shops are on the street?
faq.answer: Mostly small independent food shops and cafés rather than chains — it is a working neighbourhood street.

faq.question: How do I get to Rue des Chartreux?
faq.answer: Metro to De Brouckère (about 8 minutes' walk), or walk about 10 minutes from Grand Place via Rue au Beurre.

faq.question: Is the street busy?
faq.answer: Quiet in the morning, busier in the afternoon when shoppers spill over from Rue Neuve. It is never crowded like Grand Place.
